title: How do we find the prime factorisation of seventy two?
description: Seventy two is written as twelve times six, and each of the two factors is already broken into primes. The board puts the primes together into one row. Keeko doubts this and says twelve times six is already a prime factorisation.
teaching_notes: One idea: break each factor into primes and put all the primes into one row to get the prime factorisation of the whole number. Watch for students who stop while a composite factor such as twelve is still there.

video_script.why: The child sees that the prime factorisation of a number comes from putting together the primes of its two factors.
video_script.substitution: the book's own number, seventy two, written as twelve times six
video_script.anchor: the number seventy two written as twelve times six, with the rows of primes of twelve and of six
video_script.wrong_answer: twelve times six is already the prime factorisation of seventy two
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko thinks that twelve times six is a prime factorisation, though twelve and six are not prime.
video_script.payoff_line: Putting the primes of twelve and six together gives the prime factorisation of seventy two

final_answer.spoken: two times two times three times two times three, or two times two times two times three times three

maths_rules: the primes of 12 and of 6 put together: 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 × 3
multiplying in any order gives the same number, so 2 × 2 × 3 × 2 × 3 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3
video_script.design: The number seventy two splits into twelve and six. Their rows of primes are lifted into one long row.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the number seventy two.
<bookmark mark='split'/>Seventy two is twelve times six. Twelve is two times two times three, and six is two times three.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>What is the prime factorisation of seventy two?

beats.on_screen: the number and its two rows stay on the board; Keeko sits at the corner of the board as the child

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

carries_over: the number and its two rows

marks.term: the words prime factorisation appear with their meaning

narration: <bookmark mark='term'/>Writing a number as a multiplication of primes is called its prime factorisation.
<bookmark mark='rows'/>Twelve ends in the row two, two, three, and six ends in the row two, three.

marks.given: the numbers are written under the word Given

narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, seventy two is twelve times six. Twelve is two times two times three, and six is two times three.

beats.on_screen: To find: the prime factorisation of 72
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find the prime factorisation of seventy two.

beats.on_screen: Step 1: write the primes of each factor: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 and 6 = 2 × 3
narration: <bookmark mark='twelve'/>Step one, write the primes of each factor. Twelve gives two times two times three.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 72 = 12 × 6, so put the primes of 12 and the primes of 6 into one row: (2 × 2 × 3) joined to (2 × 3)

marks.join: the row of 12 and the row of 6 slide next to each other and a multiply sign joins them

narration: <bookmark mark='join'/>Step two, put the primes together. The primes of twelve and the primes of six go into one row, joined by multiplying.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: multiplying in any order gives the same number, so the three 2s can come first and the two 3s last

marks.twos: the three 2s are circled in teal, the two 3s in amber

narration: <bookmark mark='order'/>Step three, remember that multiplying in any order gives the same number.
<bookmark mark='twos'/>The twos can move to the front, and the threes to the back.

marks.also: the same row rearranged, 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3, appears beside it

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Putting the primes of twelve and six together gives the prime factorisation of seventy two. It is two times two times three times two times three.
<bookmark mark='also'/>Rearranged, it is two times two times two times three times three.

narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble says 12 × 6 is already the prime factorisation of 72; 12 and 6 are flagged as not prime; the bubble is struck through in the warning colour

marks.look: 12 and 6 are flagged as not prime, with 2 × 2 × 3 shown under 12

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks twelve times six is already the prime factorisation of seventy two.
<bookmark mark='look'/>But twelve is not prime, because two times two times three makes it.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>A prime factorisation holds only primes, so twelve and six must break further.
